title: NYC's Indian-Origin Mayor Is Under Fire for an Immigrant Map That Erased Little Italy, Irish, and Jewish New York
excerpt: Zohran Mamdani's well-intentioned immigrant heritage project sparked outrage by omitting iconic European-immigrant neighborhoods — exposing how even progressive diversity efforts can erase history.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Mayor Mamdani's immigrant map sparked outrage for omitting key European neighborhoods.
  • Critics argue the map reflects post-1965 immigration patterns, ignoring historical contributions.
  • The administration plans to update the map to include omitted neighborhoods by July's end.
  • The controversy highlights tensions in American identity politics regarding immigrant narratives.
  • Reactions within the Indian American community are mixed, reflecting broader diversity challenges.
Map Controversy Overview
›Original map launched in June 2023.
›Omitted neighborhoods include Little Italy, Woodlawn, and Borough Park.
›Criticism came from both progressive and conservative leaders.
›Mayor acknowledged gaps and promised updates by end of July.
The map was supposed to celebrate New York City's immigrant soul. Instead, it ignited a firestorm about whose immigration story counts. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration launched an interactive digital map in late June titled *New York: Built by Immigrants*, intended to showcase the neighborhoods, cultural landmarks, and historical contributions of immigrant communities across all five boroughs. The project, developed by the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs in partnership with the NYC Department of Cultural Affairs, was meant to be a flagship initiative of Mamdani's first year in office. But within days of its public release, the map faced a torrent of criticism for what it left out: Little Italy in Manhattan, the historically Irish enclaves of Woodlawn in the Bronx and Rockaway in Queens, the Jewish communities of Borough Park and Williamsburg in Brooklyn, and the Polish neighborhood of Greenpoint — all conspicuously absent from a map purporting to tell the full story of immigrant New York. ## The Backlash City Council member Robert Holden, who represents a Queens district with deep Irish and Italian roots, called the omissions "a slap in the face to millions of New Yorkers whose families built this city brick by brick." In a press conference on the steps of City Hall, Holden was joined by representatives from the Italian American Museum, the Irish Arts Center, and the Museum of Jewish Heritage. "You cannot tell the story of immigration in New York City and leave out Ellis Island's children," said Joseph Scelsa, president emeritus of the Italian American Museum. "Little Italy isn't just a tourist attraction — it's where my grandparents started their American life." The criticism cut across political lines. Progressive Council member Shekar Krishnan, who represents Jackson Heights — a neighborhood that *was* featured on the map — acknowledged the problem. "Inclusion means everyone. You can't build a map of immigrant New York that only reflects immigration patterns after 1965." That year is significant: the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 abolished the national-origins quota system that had favored European immigration, opening the door to large-scale migration from Asia, Latin America, and Africa. Critics allege the map's framework was built around post-1965 immigration patterns, effectively rendering a century of European immigration invisible. ## The Administration's Response The Mayor's Office initially defended the map, with a spokesperson telling reporters that it "highlights communities that have historically been underrepresented in the city's narrative." But as the backlash grew — amplified by viral social media posts and critical editorials in the *New York Post*, *Daily News*, and *The Forward* — Mamdani personally intervened. In a statement released on July 8, the mayor acknowledged the gaps. "The map was always intended to be a living document, not a finished product," Mamdani said. "We hear the criticism, and we will be updating it to include neighborhoods and communities that should have been there from the start." The updated version, the administration said, would be released by the end of July and would include Little Italy, Woodlawn, Borough Park, Greenpoint, and other historically European-immigrant neighborhoods. The city also announced the formation of an advisory panel that would include representatives from Italian, Irish, Jewish, Polish, and Greek heritage organizations. ## A Familiar Fault Line The controversy touches a raw nerve in American identity politics: the question of whether European-descended Americans — whose families may have arrived as impoverished, discriminated-against immigrants a century ago — are still "immigrants" in any politically meaningful sense, or whether that term has been implicitly redefined to mean non-white newcomers. For Indian Americans and other post-1965 diaspora communities, the debate is a reminder that diversity politics can be a double-edged sword. "We fight to be seen, to be included in the American story," said Sayu Bhojwani, founder of New American Leaders and a naturalized citizen born in Belize to Indian parents. "But that fight loses its moral authority the moment it erases someone else's story."

The incident also puts Mamdani — who has leaned heavily into his own immigrant narrative as the son of the renowned scholar Mahmood Mamdani — in an awkward position. His personal story, rooted in the Indian diaspora's journey through East Africa, was central to his mayoral campaign. Being accused of erasing other immigrant stories undermines the very universalism he campaigned on. ## What the Diaspora Is Saying Reactions within the Indian American community have been mixed. Some see the map as a well-intentioned effort that simply needs refinement. Others worry it feeds into a narrative that South Asian and other newer immigrant communities are advancing at the expense of older ones. "This is exactly the kind of thing that gets weaponized against us," said one Indian American community leader in Queens who asked not to be named. "Some guy on talk radio is already saying the Indian mayor only cares about Indian and Chinese immigrants. That's not true, but the map made it easy to say." On social media, the debate has been fierce. A post on X by journalist Reihan Salam — himself of Bangladeshi descent — calling the original map "an unforced error that plays into the worst stereotypes about progressive diversity politics" was shared thousands of times. ## What Comes Next The revised map is expected by month's end. But the episode has already left a mark on Mamdani's young administration, revealing how fraught the politics of recognition can be in a city where over 3 million residents are foreign-born and virtually every neighborhood claims an immigrant founding story. For the Indian diaspora watching from across the country, it is a case study in a challenge that will only grow as South Asian Americans assume more prominent roles in public life: how to champion inclusivity without inadvertently creating new exclusions. *Sources: NYC Mayor's Office statement (July 8, 2026), New York Post, The Forward, City & State NY, NBC New York*
image_caption: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who took office in January 2026, has faced his first major cultural controversy over the city's interactive immigrant heritage map.
nri_angle: Mamdani, born in Uganda to a family of Indian and Ugandan descent, is NYC's first mayor of South Asian heritage. The controversy highlights how immigrant identity politics in America's most diverse city directly affect how diaspora communities — including Indian Americans — see their history represented in public institutions.
